## Introduction

In this case study, I looked at simulations of tiny particles, such as water droplets in clouds for example, moving through turbulent air. Understanding how they form clusters can help explain things like how rain forms. The data set has 89 simulation runs with three input variables, that includes the Reynolds number (Re) which measures how turbulent the flow is, the Froude number (Fr) which tells how strong gravity is, and the Stokes number (St) which measures how much inertia the particles have. And for each run, I looked at four summary statistics, that includes the mean which is the average cluster volume, the variance which measures how much the cluster volumes differ from the average, the skewness which describes whether the distribution is more spread out toward smaller or larger clusters, and the kurtosis which tells us how likely the distribution is to contain unusually large clusters. For this case study, I mainly interested in inference, meaning which inputs change the cluster volumes, how big these effects are, whether they are linear or not, and whether they are all the same for all four summary statistics along with predictions for new combinations of Re, Fr, and St.

A fair question is why scientists may need a machine learning model when they already have a scientific model, which is the simulation itself. Well these simulations are very expensive, which is why there are only 89 runs for the training data, and that there is no simple formula for how the summary statistics depend on Re, Fr, and St together, so this relationship has to be learned from the data. The raw simulation results alone are also insufficient since each setting was tested only once, so it makes it difficult to isolate the effects of individual input variables. So by using information from all 89 runs, our machine learning model can better identify these relationships and can provide more accurate predictions.

Since inference is one of my main goals, I used interpretable log-scale linear models where each term helps explain the effects of the input variables through confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. With only 89 runs, the data cannot reliably support every possible model term, so variable selection is important for identifying which input variables have the greatest influence on the results. To address this, I evaluated the log transformation using Box-Cox, used natural splines to capture nonlinear relationships with St and retained only the interaction terms that were statistically significant and improved cross-validation performance.

## Methodology

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(glmnet)
library(splines)

train <- read.csv("data/data-train.csv")
test  <- read.csv("data/data-test.csv")

m1 <- train$R_moment_1; m2 <- train$R_moment_2
m3 <- train$R_moment_3; m4 <- train$R_moment_4
train$mean     <- m1
train$variance <- m2 - m1^2
train$skewness <- (m3 - 3*m1*m2 + 2*m1^3) / train$variance^1.5
train$kurtosis <- (m4 - 4*m1*m3 + 6*m1^2*m2 - 3*m1^4) / train$variance^2

prep <- function(d) {
  d$Re_f   <- factor(d$Re, levels = c(90, 224, 398))
  d$Fr_f   <- factor(d$Fr, levels = c(0.052, 0.3, Inf),
                     labels = c("0.052", "0.3", "Inf"))
  d$log_St <- log(d$St)
  d$Grav   <- factor(ifelse(d$Fr == 0.052, "strong", "weak/none"),
                     levels = c("weak/none", "strong"))
  d
}
train <- prep(train)
test  <- prep(test)

train <- train |>
  mutate(log_mean = log(mean), log_variance = log(variance),
         log_skewness = log(skewness), log_kurtosis = log(kurtosis))
responses <- c(Mean = "log_mean", Variance = "log_variance",
               Skewness = "log_skewness", Kurtosis = "log_kurtosis")

long <- train |>
  select(St, log_St, Re_f, Fr_f, mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) |>
  pivot_longer(mean:kurtosis, names_to = "target", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(target = factor(target,
                         levels = c("mean", "variance", "skewness", "kurtosis"),
                         labels = c("Mean", "Variance", "Skewness", "Kurtosis")))

fr_cols <- c("0.052" = "#D55E00", "0.3" = "#0072B2", "Inf" = "#009E73")
```

### Preparing the data

The data contains the first four raw moments of the cluster volumes in which I used to calculate the mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis. All four summary statistics have a huge range, such as the variance ranges from about $10^{-4}$ to $10^{3}$, thus I need to transform them. To pick a transformation, I sued the Box-Cox method, which just finds the power $\lambda$ that best fits the data where $\lambda = 0$ means taking the log. For all four summary statistics, the best $\lambda$ was very close to 0 and the log transformation also had a lower CV error than the other options that I tried. So I took the log of each summary statistic which also makes each effect easy to read as how many times larger or smaller a summary statistics has become. Re and Fr only have three values each, so I treated them as categorical, while St has 14 values bunched near 0, so I used $\log(St)$. One limitation of doing this method is that categorical Re and Fr mean my models can only predict and make inference at the simulated values, not for values that were not tested.

### What I saw in the data

The figure below showcases the result from all 89 simulation runs for each of the four summary statistics. Each line connects runs with the same Fr level, which allows me to see how St affects the results while Re and Fr remain constant. The figure showed me three important things about the data. The first observation is that the relationship with St is not linear even after taking $\log(St)$. The second observation is that Re and Fr seem to interact. It is seen that strong gravity ($Fr = 0.052$) greatly increases the variance, skewness, and kurtosis at $Re = 90$, but it increases less at $Re = 224$ and it barely increases at $Re = 398$. The third observation is that the lines for $Fr = 0.3$ and $Fr = \infty$ are almost identical.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(long, aes(log_St, log(value), color = Fr_f)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(target ~ Re_f, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(Re_f = function(x) paste("Re =", x))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = fr_cols, name = "Fr") +
  labs(x = "log(St)", y = "log(summary)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Models I tried

I started with a simple linear model and then I kept increasing its complexity. Model 1 is linear in St, Re, and gravity, and model 2 is similar but uses $\log(St)$ instead. Model 3 uses a cubic polynomial in $\log(St)$. Model 4 adds an Re $\times$ gravity interaction on top of model 3, and model 5 is similar to model 4 but it also adds an St $\times$ gravity interaction. Model 6 is the most flexible as it fits a separate St curve for each of the 6 Re-gravity combinations, while model 7 and 8 are lasso and ridge versions of model 6 that shrink its coefficients to prevent overfitting. I chose the lasso and ridge penalty with cross-validation and then fit each model separately for each summary statistic.

### Picking the best model

I compared all the models with 10-fold cross-validation. I measured RMSE on the log scale, meaning that an RMSE of 0.1 meant that the predictions are usually off by roughly 10%. Since I wanted my models to be interpretable, I picked the simplest model that did nearly as well as the best one.

### Final Model

The final models that I selected were model 4 and model 5. The equation below is model 4. Let $x = \log(St)$. Let $R_{224} = 1$ if $Re = 224$ and $R_{398} = 1$ if $Re = 398$ (both would be 0 if Re = 90). And let $G = 1$ for strong gravity while $G = 0$ is for weak or no gravity.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\text{summary}) = \; & \underbrace{b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2 + \dots + b_d x^d}_{\text{curved effect of St}}
+ \underbrace{b_{224} R_{224} + b_{398} R_{398}}_{\text{effect of Re}} \\
& + \underbrace{b_G \, G}_{\text{effect of gravity}}
+ \underbrace{b_{224,G} \, R_{224} G + b_{398,G} \, R_{398} G}_{\text{Re} \times \text{gravity}}
+ \varepsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

The $x$ terms make the St curve, $b_{224}$ and $b_{398}$ shift this curve for $Re = 224$ or $398$, $b_G$ shifts the curve for strong gravity, and $b_{224,G}$ and $b_{398,G}$ allow the effect of gravity to be different at each Re level. For the mean, the best model is model 5, which is the same equation as above plus an St $\times$ gravity interaction. $d$ represents how curvy the St curve can be, and is chosen by trying $d = 1$ to $6$ and keeping the lowest CV error.

## Results

### Which model predicts the best?

```{r}

library(glmnet)

train <- train |>
  mutate(log_mean = log(mean), log_variance = log(variance),
         log_skewness = log(skewness), log_kurtosis = log(kurtosis))
responses <- c(Mean = "log_mean", Variance = "log_variance",
               Skewness = "log_skewness", Kurtosis = "log_kurtosis")

rhs <- c(M1 = "St + Re_f + Grav",
         M2 = "log_St + Re_f + Grav",
         M3 = "poly(log_St, 3) + Re_f + Grav",
         M4 = "poly(log_St, 3) + Re_f * Grav",
         M5 = "poly(log_St, 3) * Grav + Re_f * Grav",
         M6 = "poly(log_St, 3) * Re_f * Grav")
x_matrix <- function(d)
  model.matrix(~ poly(log_St, 3, raw = TRUE) * Re_f * Grav, data = d)[, -1]

set.seed(325)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(train)))
cv_rmse <- function(y, m) {
  pred <- numeric(nrow(train))
  for (k in 1:10) {
    tr <- train[folds != k, ]; te <- train[folds == k, ]
    if (m %in% names(rhs)) {
      fit <- lm(as.formula(paste(y, "~", rhs[[m]])), data = tr)
      pred[folds == k] <- predict(fit, newdata = te)
    } else {
      set.seed(k)
      fit <- cv.glmnet(x_matrix(tr), tr[[y]], alpha = ifelse(m == "M7", 1, 0))
      pred[folds == k] <- predict(fit, x_matrix(te), s = "lambda.min")
    }
  }
  sqrt(mean((train[[y]] - pred)^2))
}
models <- c(names(rhs), "M7", "M8")
cv_table <- sapply(responses, function(y) sapply(models, function(m) cv_rmse(y, m)))

final_formulas <- list(
  Mean     = log_mean     ~ poly(log_St, 4) * Grav + Re_f * Grav,  # M5, d = 4
  Variance = log_variance ~ poly(log_St, 4) + Re_f * Grav,         # M4, d = 4
  Skewness = log_skewness ~ poly(log_St, 2) + Re_f * Grav,         # M4, d = 2
  Kurtosis = log_kurtosis ~ poly(log_St, 2) + Re_f * Grav          # M4, d = 2
)
final_fits <- lapply(final_formulas, lm, data = train)

final_cv <- sapply(names(final_formulas), function(t) {
  pred <- numeric(nrow(train))
  for (k in 1:10) {
    fit <- lm(final_formulas[[t]], data = train[folds != k, ])
    pred[folds == k] <- predict(fit, newdata = train[folds == k, ])
  }
  sqrt(mean((train[[responses[[t]]]] - pred)^2))
})
```

```{r}

model_labels <- c(M1 = "M1: linear", M2 = "M2: log(St)",
                  M3 = "M3: cubic in log(St)", M4 = "M4: + Re x gravity",
                  M5 = "M5: + St x gravity", M6 = "M6: separate curves",
                  M7 = "M7: lasso", M8 = "M8: ridge")
tab <- as.data.frame(round(cv_table, 3))
tab <- rbind(tab, "Final model" = round(final_cv, 3))
rownames(tab) <- c(model_labels[models], "Final model")
knitr::kable(tab)
```

The table shows the CV error for each model. So using the $\log(St)$ and adding a curved relationship with St in model 2 and model 3 does help a little, but the big improvement comes from model 4's Re $\times$ gravity interaction which cuts the CV error by more than half for the variance (1.69 to 0.79), skewness (0.62 to 0.23), and kurtosis (1.20 to 0.41). For the mean, model 5 does even better, which lowers the CV error from 0.101 to 0.074. I need to consider the bias-variance tradeoff where models 1 through 3 are too simple which results in high bias, while more complex models like model 6 fits noise which results in high variance and would make the CV error for the mean to go back up.

The table above displays models 3 through 6 that uses a third-degree polynomial of $\log(St)$. Testing degrees 1 to 6, the table from the appendix shows that degree 4 is the best for the mean (model 5) and the variance (model 4), and degree 2 is the best for skewness and kurtosis (both model 4), which gives me the final model as seen in the last row of the table above.

For uncertainty, the predictions are typically off by a factor of $e^{\text{CV error}}$, which works out to about 8% for the mean ($e^{0.074} \approx 1.08$), 25% for skewness, 50% for kurtosis, and a factor of 2 for the variance. Do note that predictions are less reliable for test points whose St falls outside the range of values used to build the models for their corresponding Re and Fr settings.

## How Re, gravity, and St affects the clusters

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
settings <- unique(train[, c("Re", "Fr", "Re_f", "Fr_f", "Grav")])
st_range <- train |> group_by(Re, Fr) |>
  summarise(st_min = min(St), st_max = max(St), .groups = "drop")
grid <- merge(settings, data.frame(St = exp(seq(log(0.05), log(3), length.out = 60)))) |>
  left_join(st_range, by = c("Re", "Fr")) |>
  filter(St >= st_min, St <= st_max)        # only where we have data
grid$log_St <- log(grid$St)

curves <- bind_rows(lapply(names(final_fits), function(t) {
  cbind(grid, target = t, fit = exp(predict(final_fits[[t]], newdata = grid)))
}))
curves$target <- factor(curves$target, levels = names(responses))

ggplot(curves, aes(St, fit, color = Fr_f)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = long, aes(St, value, color = Fr_f), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 0.6) +
  facet_grid(target ~ Re_f, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(Re_f = function(x) paste("Re =", x))) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3)) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = fr_cols, name = "Fr") +
  labs(x = "St (log scale)", y = "Summary (log scale)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}

setting <- function(St, Re, Fr) prep(data.frame(St = St, Re = Re, Fr = Fr))
fold_change <- function(fit, a, b) {
  ratio <- unname(exp(predict(fit, newdata = a) - predict(fit, newdata = b)))
  format(signif(ratio, 3), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
}
comparisons <- list(
  "Re 90 to 224"                   = list(setting(0.5, 224, Inf),   setting(0.5, 90, Inf)),
  "Re 224 to 398"                  = list(setting(0.5, 398, Inf),   setting(0.5, 224, Inf)),
  "Strong vs. no gravity, Re 90"   = list(setting(0.5, 90, 0.052),  setting(0.5, 90, Inf)),
  "Strong vs. no gravity, Re 224"  = list(setting(0.5, 224, 0.052), setting(0.5, 224, Inf)),
  "Strong vs. no gravity, Re 398"  = list(setting(0.5, 398, 0.052), setting(0.5, 398, Inf))
)
effects <- sapply(final_fits, function(fit)
  sapply(comparisons, function(cc) fold_change(fit, cc[[1]], cc[[2]])))
knitr::kable(effects)
```

As the table shows, it suggests that Re has the biggest effect. Increasing the Re from 90 to 224 makes the mean about 33 times smaller while the skewness becomes about 5.6 times larger, which suggests that stronger turbulence leads to smaller clusters, but there are still a few clusters much larger than the typical one that make the distribution less balanced. Another thing to note is that strong gravity does have a greater effect whenever the turbulence is weaker. From the table, strong gravity increases the variance about 765 times at $Re = 90$, only about 7 times at $Re = 224$, and lowers the variance to about half at $Re = 398$. This could mean that gravity causes particles to settle and form larger clusters while stronger turbulence breaks these clusters apart. From the plots, it appears that gravity has little effect in the mean but strongly affects variance, skewness, and kurtosis. This suggests that gravity mainly changes how much the cluster sizes differ rather than the average cluster volume.

## Conclusion

So using cross-validation, model 4 was the best simpler model for the variance, skewness, and kurtosis, while model 5 was the best for the mean since it accounts for how the relationship between St and the mean cluster volume changes with the strength of gravity. These models provide accurate predictions while staying simple enough to understand how each input variable affects the cluster volumes. However, one limitation is that some test points have St values outside the training range, so those predictions are less reliable. My main finding is that Re has the strongest effect on cluster volumes, which shrinks the average cluster volume but it raises the skewness and kurtosis. Another finding is that gravity only matters when it is strong, and its effect fades as turbulence grows. Also that gravity changes the average cluster size only slightly and mainly changes how much cluster sizes vary. And finally, St has a nonlinear effect on all four summary statistics.

## Appendix

The table below showcases CV error (in log scale) for polynomial degrees $d = 1$ to $6$, which uses model 5 for the mean and model 4 for the other summary statistics.

```{r}

deg_rhs <- c(Mean     = "poly(log_St, %d) * Grav + Re_f * Grav",  # M5
             Variance = "poly(log_St, %d) + Re_f * Grav",         # M4
             Skewness = "poly(log_St, %d) + Re_f * Grav",         # M4
             Kurtosis = "poly(log_St, %d) + Re_f * Grav")         # M4
deg_table <- sapply(names(deg_rhs), function(t) sapply(1:6, function(d) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(responses[[t]], "~", sprintf(deg_rhs[[t]], d)))
  pred <- numeric(nrow(train))
  for (k in 1:10) {
    fit <- lm(f, data = train[folds != k, ])
    pred[folds == k] <- predict(fit, newdata = train[folds == k, ])
  }
  sqrt(mean((train[[responses[[t]]]] - pred)^2))
}))
deg_table <- data.frame(d = 1:6, round(deg_table, 3))
knitr::kable(deg_table, row.names = FALSE)
```
